Photograph: Courtesy of National Santa Agency Atlanta First professional St Nick with Down’s syndrome inducted into International Santa Claus Hall of Fame Atlanta’s Bradley Carlisle first played Kris Kringle for kids with Down’s syndrome and has now completed elite Santa Academy Ramon Antonio Vargas Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 07.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google After recently gaining recognition as the first professional Santa Claus with Down’s syndrome in the US, Bradley Carlisle has already gotten a lot more than the traditional serving of milk and cookies that is usually left out for Father Christmas each year. That is because the 37-year-old community theater actor from suburban Atlanta landed an honorary induction into the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame upon completing one of the largest Christmas performer schools in the US in late August – a distinction meant to recognize the important representation his emergence on the holiday scene has brought, according to his supporters. As his mother, Debbie Chadrix, told it to the Guardian on Friday, Carlisle’s path to his unique place among what she called the Claus family began at the 2023 holiday party of the Down Syndrome Association of Atlanta (DSAA). Chadrix said the organization’s executive director approached her during the gathering and remarked: “We need a Santa with Down’s syndrome who looks like the kids” invited to the party as the guests of honor. Her cafe offered an opportunity for her daughter – and for others with intellectual disabilities Read more The group’s leader picked Carlisle because of his passion for acting on the local community theater circuit, Chadrix said. Yet Chadrix wasn’t completely sold. She said her son used to fear Santa growing up because he evidently equated jolly old St Nick ’s white gloves with those worn by healthcare providers who took care of him during nonetheless difficult medical experiences. It was only after one Santa in particular slipped his gloves off for Bradley that he warmed up to the concept, she recounted. Carlisle, however, gamely accepted the offer to transform into Santa for the next DSAA holiday party. He confidently wore the white beard and recognizable red suit, and interacted with more than 200 children involved with the DSAA. Chadrix said she has never forgotten the looks on many of those children’s faces “when they realized Bradley looked like them – and talked like them, a little bit, too”. And then Bradley declared “he would be our Santa from now on”. Local news media picked up Carlisle’s story by his second Christmas season as Santa, giving his profile a bump, Chadrix said. And he also appeared on a podcast alongside Rick Rosenthal, who runs Atlanta’s Northern Lights Santa Academy and invited Carlisle to attend a four-day course beginning on 20 August. At Rosenthal’s academy, which he described as the second largest institution of its kind in the US, Carlisle and others train to carry on in the spirit of figures such as Santa, Mrs Claus and the Christmas elves. Santas in particular receive an education on a wide range of topics, including how to properly dress for the part, adequately maintain their white beards and improvise answers to the heart-wrenching questions children can occasionally ask, especially if grappling with a terminal illness or grieving the loss of a loved one. Carlisle excelled in that atmosphere, with Chadrix proudly noting that he underwent the same program as all of the other enrollees there. And at a 23 August ceremony on the academy’s final day, Phil Wenz of the Santa Claus Oath Foundation called Carlisle up to a stage. A video on a social media account for Carlisle showed Wenz complimenting him for the confident style he had displayed while personifying Santa Claus in the lobby outside the ceremony hall. Wenz alluded to how some of Carlisle’s fellow Claus family members had banded together to cover a completely custom-made Santa suit for him. Carlisle’s photograph would also be shown in New York City’s Times Square as part of the US’s Down Syndrome Awareness Month beginning on 1 October, which is Bradley’s birthday, Wenz continued. And then Wenz revealed the pièce de résistance: he said he had consulted with a number of Christmas community heavyweights to enshrine him as an honorary member of the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. Wenz punctuated the moment with handing Carlisle a badge. Carlisle triumphantly held it up with his right hand while he smiled widely and the audience applauded. Rosenthal has belonged to that institution in the town of Santa Claus, Indiana, since late 2023. It’s something he considers one of his greatest honors in his 58 years as a Santa. And he said Carlisle merited enshrinement because of his already showing “a magnified sensitivity” to those with Down’s syndrome who are among Santa’s faithful that others in the Claus family simply cannot. Chadrix said she was notified in advance of the plan to welcome Carlisle to the International Santa Claus Hall of Fame. And she said she made clear, essentially, that she did not want Bradley’s condition to be the only reason he was being enshrined. She recalled Rosenthal assuring her: “Phil Wenz knows what he’s looking at. And as soon as he saw Bradley as Santa and talking to people and interacting, he knew he has something different and special – and that’s why he got to the hall of fame.” Among the many to congratulate Carlisle was the DSAA, which shared a link to a television news segment about him published by the Atlanta station WXIA on Thursday. “Saaaaantaaaaa we know him! So proud of our Santa Bradley,” the organization wrote, adding that those who attend Atlanta’s 3 October Buddy Walk – a DSAA fundraiser at the Kennesaw State University Marietta campus – “might see him incognito”. Carlisle told WXIA that he enjoyed being Santa “because I like to help with the kids”. The station also asked him what it feels like to slip into his Santa suit. He replied: “It feels like love.” Explore more on these topics Atlanta Down's syndrome Christmas news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty Images Nashville Man arrested in Nashville after DNA links him to unsolved 1990s rape cases Archibald Amory, 58, reportedly being held in Tennessee pending return to New York, where he was tied to two cases Edward Helmore Wed 18 Nov 2026 08.39 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 08.41 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been arrested in Nashville after DNA linked him to a series of unsolved New York City rapes from the 1990s, according to a news report. Archibald Amory, 58, was detained on Thursday in Hermitage, a neighborhood of Nashville, and is being held there pending his return to New York City, according to the Daily News , citing sources and Nashville authorities. Amory has been linked via DNA to two rapes that took place in Queens, and connected to several other uncharged sex assaults. Sources said recent advances in DNA technology and investigative methods helped identify Amory. Court papers filed in Tennessee said special victims investigators in Nashville and with the NYPD “identified Archibald Amory as a wanted fugitive in connection to a series of rape investigations originating in the jurisdiction of New York City”. Armory appeared in court in Nashville on Monday, according to a spokesperson for the district attorney of Davidson county. He is currently being held on $800,000 bond. Ex-Chicago detective identified as killing child in 65-year cold case Read more Another man has also been arrested, in Miami, for allegedly raping a woman in New York’s Central Park last month. Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, was arrested on Tuesday at a Miami Burger King where he had been working. Police said he will also be charged in two other Central Park rapes. Rivera-Deleon will be charged with the sexual assault of a 39-year-old woman who was walking just outside Central Park on 24 October when he pulled a knife on her near E 66th Street and Fifth Avenue. The suspect allegedly dragged the victim into the park, where he raped her, before a bystander, who witnessed the attack, called 911. Rivera-Deleon was identified as the attacker via surveillance film, and investigators have linked him to a Central Park rape in 2023 and another in 2021. https://www.dw.com/en/russian-ornitholog.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ph5N Prefer DW on Google Renowned Russian ornithologist Sofia Rosenfeld on an expedition Image: Privat Advertisement Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says. He lives in Israel , while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist. On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony. A biologist who dedicated her life to Arctic birds Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arctic birds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album. Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship. She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age. "Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said. Sofia and her father Boris Rosenfeld in Israel during her most recent visit Image: Privat Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft. "They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method." Protecting birds in Russia and beyond Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential. Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community. "She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us." More than 225 cases over donations to FBK across Russia In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow. Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand. "She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable". Sofia Rosenfeld during an expedition Image: Privat For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most. There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony. A year of court hearings and travel restrictions Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic. Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison." Leaving Russia was never an option "The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit. Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry. Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights. Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention. The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person." This article was originally published in Russian.
